sec.title: 6. Care Delivery, Evacuation, and Transport Logistics
sec.p: The organization of major sporting events poses challenges related to health care planning, public safety, and emergency medical response. Classified within the field of mass gathering medicine, this interdisciplinary area focuses on the health implications of events that bring together large numbers of people within a limited space and time, potentially generating health care demands that exceed local system capacity.44

In the sporting context, events such as marathons, triathlons, Olympic Games, world championships, and major football tournaments present heightened logistical complexity. These events involve not only athletes of varying ages and fitness levels but also spectators, volunteers, and support personnel. Cardiovascular emergencies represent a smaller proportion of medical incidents, yet they require immediate and highly coordinated responses.45 Such responses must be supported by integrated systems based on advanced planning, appropriate infrastructure, multidisciplinary teams, clear triage protocols, efficient communication, and hospital integration, aiming to minimize the interval between clinical collapse and definitive intervention, in accordance with the time-dependent principle of emergency care.

Sports physicians, cardiologists, orthopedists, and emergency/critical care physicians play a central role throughout this process, from pre-event planning and medical infrastructure design to immediate care delivery, stabilization of critically ill patients, and decision-making regarding evacuation and transport.

sec.title: 6.1.1. Pre-Event Risk Assessment
sec.p: Care planning should begin months before the competition and be based on a comprehensive risk assessment, including:

list-item.p: Epidemiological profile of athletes (age range, prevalence of comorbidities, competitive level);
Environmental conditions (climate, humidity, altitude, air pollution);
History of incidents in similar previous events;
Capacity of local health care services (hospitals, EMS, Fire Department).

sec.p: A qualitative study conducted at the Athens Marathon demonstrated that interorganizational knowledge transfer among health care, security, and event management stakeholders was critical for aligning triage protocols, evacuation strategies, and hospital integration.46 This interinstitutional coordination is currently regarded as a key success factor in mass gathering medicine.

sec.title: 6.1.2 Care Structure
sec.p: Medical care infrastructure should include a combination of fixed medical aid stations and mobile teams to ensure rapid access to victims at any location within the event. Recent experience supports the deployment of strategically distributed advanced medical posts (AMPs), capable of performing triage, initial stabilization, ALS, and evacuation decisions.45
AMPs must be sized to manage both critical emergencies and low-complexity complaints, thereby preventing overload of ambulances and hospital systems.

sec.title: 6.1.3 Communication and Command
sec.p: A medical command center (MCC) should integrate all information regarding incidents, available resources, team locations, and evacuation routes. Communication failures are among the leading causes of care delays in mass gathering events.44,46

Practical drills with realistic simulations of critical scenarios – such as cardiac arrest occurring along the course – significantly improve team efficiency and reduce response times. Events such as the Tokyo 2020 and Beijing 2022 Olympic Games mandated simulation-based training for all professionals involved.47

sec.title: 6.1.4 Event Operations
sec.p: The operational phase of major sporting events requires time-dependent responses to medical emergencies within a dynamic environment involving multiple interacting factors. Complexity arises from geographic dispersion of athletes, large spectator crowds, and limited access to certain areas of the courses or sporting venues.

sec.title: 6.1.5 Advanced Medical Posts
sec.p: AMPs constitute the core of medical logistics. In marathons, primary AMPs should be installed near the start and finish areas, complemented by satellite posts along the course at high-risk locations (long ascents, heat-prone areas, zones with high spectator density). In stadium-based events, AMPs should be located behind main stands, near ambulance access points.45,48

sec.title: 6.1.6 Mobile Teams
sec.p: Mobile teams play a critical role in reducing response times, and several modalities can be included:49

list-item.p: Medical cyclists: in marathons and triathlons, holding backpacks equipped with AEDs, pulse oximeters, airway supplies, and basic analgesics;
Motorcycle ambulances: useful in congested urban areas;
Boats or kayaks: for open-water or lake competitions;
Pedestrian teams: in stadiums and arenas;
4×4 vehicles: for off-road events such as adventure races or motocross;
AED-equipped drones: studies on the experimental use of drones delivering AEDs suggest potential reductions in time to defibrillation in outdoor simulated scenarios.50

sec.p: A Japanese study analyzing emergencies in sports stadiums between 2015 and 2019 found that clinically severe and potentially fatal incidents frequently occurred in places such as swimming pools, restrooms, and spectator seating areas. These results underscore the need for comprehensive medical emergency systems, including strategic AED distribution, to serve athletes, spectators, and staff alike.51

sec.title: 6.1.7 Communication and Command Center
sec.p: Operations should be centralized within an MCC, integrating communication among AMPs, mobile teams, ambulances, and referral hospitals. Standardized communication protocols are recommended to ensure clarity in the information provided. Effective communication among organizers, health services, and security is essential for incident management, reducing triage and evacuation times.46

sec.title: 6.2.1. Logistics During Medical Care
sec.p: Cardiac arrest must be recognized and treated within 3 minutes, with immediate AED use. A video-based analysis of cardiac arrest cases during sports activities showed 100% survival among athletes defibrillated within this time frame.53

ALS procedures may be initiated when trained personnel are present, but must not delay or interrupt chest compressions, AED use, or the decision to transport the athlete. Intravenous (IV) or intraosseous (IO) epinephrine (1 mg) and amiodarone (300 mg) should be administered after the third shock if the athlete remains unresponsive prior to field removal. If the rhythm converts from shockable to non-shockable for more than one CPR cycle, immediate transfer to hospital should be considered. When moving the patient is difficult, minimizing CPR interruption is critical, and continuing resuscitation on site (even after 3 shocks) may be preferable.

sec.title: 6.2.2. Documentation and Quality Indicators
sec.p: All care must be documented using standardized medical records, including symptom onset time, time to first contact, interventions performed, and outcomes. These data enable calculation of indicators such as mean time to AED application and hospital transport rates, which are essential for post-event audits.

sec.title: 6.3.1. Evacuation Criteria
sec.p: Medical evacuation decisions at sporting events should consider clinical severity, feasibility of initial on-site stabilization, and availability of specialized hospital resources. International field triage guidelines recommend priority transport for patients with higher severity criteria, such as:55,56

list-item.p: Altered mental status with Glasgow Coma Scale score ≤ 13;
Hemodynamic instability or shock unresponsive to initial measures;
Need for definitive referral hospital-based interventions (eg, catheterization for acute myocardial infarction).

sec.title: 6.3.2. Evacuation Routes
sec.p: Close coordination with post-cardiac arrest care teams is essential. Transport time to predefined destinations should be minimized. Dedicated evacuation routes must be planned in advance, avoiding intersections with athletes or spectator crowds. Interception points along the courses are recommended to facilitate rapid ambulance access. In Japan, a recent study highlighted that lack of predefined routes was a major cause of evacuation delays in mass sporting events.51

sec.title: 6.3.3. Integration with Referral Hospitals
sec.p: Referral hospitals should be notified in advance about the event, with predefined designation of units for cardiovascular, trauma, and pediatric cases. Structured prehospital notification, including updates on patient progress, allows receiving teams (who should be familiar and experienced with standardized protocols) to prepare appropriately and reduce time to intervention.46

sec.title: 6.3.4 Safe Transport
sec.p: Transport should occur only after initial stabilization of vital functions, except in situations where definitive treatment is hospital-based (eg, catheterization for ST-elevation myocardial infarction). Current guidelines discourage transport during ongoing CPR due to reduced effectiveness and increased risk of injury to rescuers performing maneuvers inside a moving vehicle; ideally, transport should occur after the victim has regained an organized rhythm. Transport during active resuscitation should be considered only when mechanical compression devices are available or when distances are minimal. Manual CPR in a moving ambulance compromises quality and exposes staff to unnecessary risk. In cases of recurrent cardiac arrest during transport, resuscitation may continue using air or ground ambulances with trained personnel, preferably using automated chest compression devices.
In suspected severe hyperthermia (> 40 °C), immediate cooling (cold-water immersion or ice towels) should precede transport ("cool first, transport second").

sec.title: 6.3.5. Monitoring During Transport

list-item.p: Continuous ECG monitoring in cardiovascular patients;
Pulse oximetry, temperature, and serial blood pressure measurements for all transports;
Capnography in ventilated patients;
Continuous communication with the receiving hospital.

sec.p: Following cardiac arrest, mild hypothermia may occur in comatose patients; active rewarming should be avoided. Hypothermia should be maintained, with targeted temperature management (32 to 36 °C) for 12 to 24 hours and active fever prevention (≤ 37.5 °C) for 72 hours. Cooling devices with temperature feedback control are preferred over prehospital cold IV fluid infusion due to the risk of recurrent arrest and pulmonary edema.

sec.title: 6.4. Legal and Safety Aspects
sec.p: It is essential to document consent or refusal of transport, ensure confidentiality of clinical data in accordance with the Brazilian General Data Protection Regulation, and guarantee operational safety of evacuation routes by preventing interference from crowds or urban traffic.48
Knowledge transfer among organizers, medical teams, emergency services, and referral hospitals is a key element in continuous improvement of care logistics.

A recent study at the Athens Marathon showed that the absence of clear protocols shared between institutions increased the risk of duplicated efforts, communication failures, and delays during critical evacuations. Implementation of prior interinstitutional meetings, joint simulations, and daily briefings during the event was associated with improved operational efficiency and reduced response times.46

Another illustrative example is the field hospital model used at the 2023 Ryder Cup, where sports physicians, cardiologists, orthopedists, and emergency physicians worked side by side in a modular care system. This structure enabled real-time data collection, later used to assess areas for improvement, such as refining ambulance positioning, medication stock management, and hyperthermia training.45

Post-event audits, including clinical outcome reports and process indicators (time to defibrillation, on-site initiation of cooling for exertional heat stroke, proportion of cases stabilized on site vs. transferred), are indispensable tools for providing feedback to the planning of future competitions.44

list-item.p: Clubs: prioritize AED placement in sports areas, with access outside training hours;
Large arenas: separate plans for athletes and spectators; resources coordinated by a medical director;

Marathons and mass events: up to 5 first responders per 1,000 athletes; at least 1 ALS-trained physician per 2,500 runners; aid stations approximately every 1.5 km; ambulances preferentially positioned in the second half of the course;
Olympic Games: multi-venue logistics; need for mobile teams and medical interpreters; joint training to standardize responses (Figure 5).

sec.title: 7. Basic and Advanced Life Support Protocols (the Chain of Survival) Adapted to Sports Settings
sec.p: Cardiac arrest in athletes, although uncommon, is a catastrophic event that requires an immediate, coordinated, and efficient response. Adapting the AHA "Chain of Survival" to the sports environment is essential to improve outcomes.25,56-59

sec.title: 7.1. Immediate Recognition and Activation of Emergency Medical Services

list-item.p: Sports-specific adaptation: sudden collapse may be difficult to distinguish from other conditions (eg, extreme fatigue, seizure, trauma). The guiding principle is to treat any collapsed, unresponsive athlete as having cardiac arrest until proven otherwise;

Action: Check responsiveness (shake shoulders and shout). If there is no response, call for help loudly and immediately activate the local EMS (SAMU 192 in Brazil). Assign a specific individual to place the call. Request an AED. In sports venues, the AED must be accessible and signposted, with an ideal access time of less than 3 minutes.

Sports-specific adaptation: CPR may be initiated immediately by trained individuals present on site (coaches, athletic trainers, trained teammates, referees, or even athletes). The technique follows standard AHA and SBC recommendations;
Action (basic):
Open the airway (head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver);
Check breathing; if absent or agonal gasping is present, begin chest compressions;
Chest compressions at a rate of 100–120/min, with a depth of 5–6 cm, allowing complete chest wall recoil. Minimize interruptions;
Ventilations: if trained and willing, provide a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio; if untrained or unwilling, perform continuous chest compressions only.
Sports-specific adaptation: VF is the most common cause of sudden cardiac arrest in athletes. Shock administration is the only effective treatment. AED should be applied within 3 minutes;
Action (basic/advanced):
Turn on the AED and follow voice prompts.
Expose the chest and quickly dry excessive sweat, if necessary, to ensure proper electrode adhesion.
Ensure that no one is touching the victim during rhythm analysis and shock delivery; administer the shock if advised and immediately resume CPR.

sec.title: 7.4. Advanced Life Support and Post-Cardiac Arrest Care

list-item.p: Sports-specific adaptation: provided by the on-site EMS team, while the host sports organization must facilitate ambulance access and ensure transfer to a predesignated referral hospital;
Action (advanced – by health care professionals):
Advanced airway management: endotracheal intubation or supraglottic airway placement to ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation;
Vascular access: establish IO or IV access for medication administration;
Pharmacologic therapy: administer epinephrine (1 mg) IV/IO every 3–5 minutes during CPR. If VF/VT persists, consider amiodarone (300 mg) IV/IO;

Management of reversible causes – the 5Hs (hypovolemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, hydrogen ion/acidosis, hypo-/hyperkalemia) and 5Ts (toxins, tamponade [cardiac], tension pneumothorax, thrombosis [coronary], thromboembolism [pulmonary]): in sports settings, one should strongly suspect:
– Commotio cordis: blunt chest trauma (eg, ball impact). The treatment is immediate defibrillation;
– Hypothermia/hyperthermia: in endurance sports;
– Electrolyte disturbances: severe dehydration.

Post-resuscitation care: after ROSC, initiate ventilatory support, targeted temperature management (32–36 °C – therapeutic hypothermia), and rapid transport to a hospital with percutaneous coronary intervention capability and comprehensive care.

sec.title: 7.5. Site-specific protocol for training and competition venues

list-item.p: Prevention: cardiovascular screening (medical history and physical examination) to identify athletes at increased risk;
Preparation: ensure the presence of a trained response team and the availability of a functional AED with charged batteries. A written action plan must be in place and known to all staff;
Simulation: conduct regular training sessions and simulation drills (every 6 months) involving all personnel, from security staff to physicians.
